analysis.one_liner: Strips mortgage-interest and depreciation tax breaks from owners of 50+ single-family rentals.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote since it was introduced in March 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the tax code so that any taxpayer owning 50 or more single-family rental homes (homes with four or fewer units) loses two major write-offs on those homes: the deduction for mortgage interest and the deduction for depreciation. Small landlords stay untouched, and owners can keep the deductions on newly built rentals and on low-income-housing-tax-credit properties. The tax break also comes back for one year if the owner sells the home to a family that will live in it, a nonprofit, a land bank, a resident-owned cooperative, or a community land trust — steering big investors toward selling houses rather than holding them as rentals.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in neighborhoods where large investors have bought up single-family homes, and aspiring homebuyers who compete with those investors' all-cash offers. The bill is a tax increase on large corporate landlords, designed to make holding single-family homes as long-term rentals less profitable and selling them to owner-occupants more attractive. Small landlords with fewer than 50 properties are not affected.

how_it_helps.text: Any taxpayer owning 50 or more single-family rental properties, counting affiliated companies as one owner, would lose the federal deduction for interest paid on debt connected to those properties.
The same large owners would also lose the depreciation deduction on those properties, eliminating two of the main tax shelters that make large-scale single-family rentals profitable.
Small landlords are untouched: the threshold is 50 properties, so individual and family landlords below it keep all current deductions.

Owners regain the interest and depreciation deductions in the year they sell a home to an individual who will use it as a principal residence, or to a nonprofit affordable-housing group, community land trust, land bank, resident-owned cooperative, or public-housing-agency subsidiary — a carve-out intended to push homes toward homeownership.

Newly constructed rentals and properties qualifying for the low-income housing tax credit are exempt, so the bill targets investors buying up existing housing stock rather than builders creating new units.

analysis.who_pays: Large investors in single-family rentals — institutional landlords that own hundreds or thousands of detached homes and townhouses — would pay substantially more federal tax by losing interest and depreciation deductions on those holdings. The bill's authors intend for that cost to change investor behavior: hold fewer existing homes, sell more to owner-occupants, or build new instead.

drawbacks.text: Economists and industry critics of this approach argue that raising landlords' after-tax costs can be passed through to tenants as higher rents, or can shrink the supply of single-family rental homes in markets where renting is the realistic option. The bill does not cap rents or require any savings to be passed to tenants.

The exemptions are broad enough that large operators could restructure around the bill: newly built single-family rentals are fully exempt, so a large investor can keep every deduction by shifting toward build-to-rent development, and the bill does not stop acquisitions of existing homes by owners just under the 50-property threshold.
The deduction disallowance applies only to debt incurred and property placed in service after enactment, so it phases in gradually rather than immediately changing existing large portfolios.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people, the upside is real but indirect and geographically uneven: it changes the economics for investors in exactly the single-family markets where investor competition is strongest, and its sale-year carve-out rewards selling to families. The honest downside is that a tax increase on landlords is not a guarantee of lower rents — in tight markets, some of the cost could reach tenants — and the new-construction exemption lets big operators keep a growing slice of the market with full deductions. On balance it is a targeted, moderate measure: it does not ban corporate ownership of homes, but it removes two large subsidies for doing so at scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Raphael Warnock introduced S. 969, the Stop Predatory Investing Act, in the Senate on March 11, 2025.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further action since then.
Twelve senators cosponsored the bill: 11 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate Independents; no Republican cosponsored.

The bill would deny interest and depreciation deductions to taxpayers owning 50 or more single-family residential rental properties, with exemptions for low-income-housing-tax-credit properties, newly constructed rentals, and sales to owner-occupants or affordable-housing organizations.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate landlords of single-family homes are better off, because they keep the interest and depreciation deductions the bill would have removed and face no new tax. Renters and would-be homebuyers are no worse off than before, but no better either, since the bill never advanced. Small landlords also keep their advantage over large competitors.

for.name: Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 12 cosponsors.

for.name: 11 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Smith, Wyden, Baldwin, Warren, Gallego, Reed, Klobuchar, Welch, Blumenthal, and Booker, among others.

against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill has sat referred to the committee since the day it was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents and no Republican has signed on; the Senate's 55-seat Republican majority controls the Finance Committee, where the bill has sat without action.

industries.note: They would lose interest and depreciation deductions on every single-family rental above the 50-property threshold, directly raising the cost of buying up existing homes to rent out — the practice the bill targets. Their gain in the status quo comes from converting owner-occupied housing into rentals, which competes directly with families trying to buy.

Newly constructed single-family rentals are exempt, so these operators keep full deductions while competitors holding existing homes lose them — a relative advantage that could accelerate large-scale build-to-rent development, which still adds rental supply rather than homes for sale.
Properties eligible for LIHTC are exempt from the disallowance, so affordable-housing developers keep their deductions unaffected.
They keep all current deductions unchanged, and would gain a relative advantage over large competitors who lose theirs — leveling a tax playing field that currently favors the biggest owners.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, no Republican cosponsors, and the bill sitting in a Republican-chaired Finance Committee for the rest of 2025 with no hearing or markup, it is very unlikely to advance this Congress. A similar version stalled the same way in the previous Congress; the realistic path forward would be attachment to a broader tax bill, which its current support level does not suggest.
